title: An Indian-American CEO Laid Off 1,600 Xbox Workers. Days Later, the Fed Appointed Her to an Advisory Panel. The Internet Did the Rest.
excerpt: Asha Sharma was born in Wisconsin, ran Instacart through its IPO, and was personally chosen by Satya Nadella to lead Xbox. None of that stopped critics from reducing her to her ethnicity.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft laid off 1,600 Xbox employees amid a larger 4,800-job restructuring.
  • Asha Sharma, who oversaw the layoffs, was appointed to a Federal Reserve advisory panel.
  • Critics targeted Sharma's ethnicity, linking it to the H-1B visa controversy.
  • Sharma's leadership experience includes roles at Instacart and Meta, complicating the narrative against her.
  • The incident highlights ongoing racial scapegoating in discussions about immigration and job loss.

Microsoft's Xbox division laid off 1,600 employees on Monday as part of a sweeping 4,800-job restructuring. Two days later, the woman who signed the layoff memo — Indian-American executive Asha Sharma — was appointed to a newly created Federal Reserve task force on "Productivity and Jobs." The collision of those two events has made Sharma a lightning rod in America's escalating fight over immigration, outsourcing, and who gets to lead. ## The Layoffs and the Optics The numbers alone are stark. Microsoft said it would eliminate 3,200 positions within Xbox's gaming division over the current fiscal year, with 1,600 cuts taking immediate effect. Four studios — Compulsion Games, Double Fine Productions, Ninja Theory, and Undead Labs — will be divested or spun off. Meanwhile, Microsoft had been approved earlier this year to hire 2,273 foreign H-1B visa employees, according to U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services data. The juxtaposition — thousands of Americans let go, thousands of H-1B approvals on the books — sparked a firestorm. "This is INSANE. LEGAL immigration is a major problem," said Representative Riley Moore, a West Virginia Republican. "These companies, especially big tech, are abusing these immigration programs to replace American workers with foreign workers. No more. It's long past time to end the H-1B scam." Microsoft disputed the framing. "These decisions are based on business need, not visa status," a spokesperson said. "H-1B employees were also impacted by job eliminations in the U.S." > **"CEO Satya Nadella personally tapped her to run Xbox in February, calling her platform-scaling expertise "critical" for the gaming business."** ## Then Came the Fed Appointment On Thursday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh announced several new advisory task forces. Sharma was named to the "Productivity and Jobs" panel alongside Andreessen Horowitz co-founder Marc Andreessen and Stanford economist Charles I. Jones. Warsh described the appointees as "the best minds from a range of disciplines" who would help "sharpen our performance as an institution." The announcement made no mention of the Xbox layoffs or the H-1B controversy. Critics pounced. "It's like asking El Chapo to lead the DEA," one X user wrote. Others called the appointment "totally unexplainable" and accused the Fed of trying to "incentivize" mass layoffs of American workers. ## The Racial Targeting of an American-Born Executive What followed was uglier. Some critics openly targeted Sharma's Indian heritage — despite the fact that she was born and raised in Wisconsin. "Her one function is to purge white Americans and replace them with Indian cheap foreign labor," one widely shared post read, conflating Sharma's ethnicity with the broader H-1B debate.
Asha Sharma's Leadership Journey
›Born and raised in Wisconsin.
›Led Instacart through its IPO.
›Former VP at Meta.
›Appointed by Satya Nadella to lead Xbox.
The pattern is not new. Indian-American executives in Silicon Valley — from Satya Nadella at Microsoft to Sundar Pichai at Google — have faced similar accusations whenever their companies make workforce decisions. But the timing of Sharma's layoffs, arriving days after Vice President JD Vance announced a major H-1B fraud investigation, turned her into a proxy for the entire debate. Sharma's résumé complicates the "unqualified outsider" narrative. She studied at the University of Minnesota's Carlson School of Management, served as chief operating officer at Instacart — where she steered the company through its IPO — and held vice-presidential roles at Meta before rejoining Microsoft to lead its CoreAI product division. CEO Satya Nadella personally tapped her to run Xbox in February, calling her platform-scaling expertise "critical" for the gaming business. ## Why Diaspora Communities Should Watch This Closely The Sharma saga sits at the intersection of three forces reshaping life for Indian Americans. First, the Trump administration's aggressive posture on H-1B visas: Vance's Department of Labor has launched "dozens of subpoenas and investigations" into visa fraud, and a federal judge recently struck down a $100,000 H-1B application fee the administration had imposed by executive order. Second, the rising visibility of Indian-origin leaders in corporate America. Sharma joins Nadella, Pichai, Adobe's Shantanu Narayen, and Palo Alto Networks' Nikesh Arora on a growing roster of Indian-descent executives running major U.S. companies. That visibility makes them targets when nativist sentiment spikes.
Racial Targeting in Corporate America
›Critics linked Sharma's ethnicity to job cuts.
›Similar accusations faced by other Indian-American executives.
›Rising nativist sentiment impacts visibility of Indian-origin leaders.
›The incident reflects ongoing racial scapegoating.
Third, the gaming industry's broader crisis. Microsoft spent over $20 billion on Xbox content and platform investments over five years, but annual revenue fell by nearly half a billion over the same period. Game Pass stalled at 30 million subscribers. Rising memory chip prices forced console price hikes. The restructuring Sharma is executing has roots in a failed strategy she inherited, not one she designed. None of that context made it into the viral posts equating her heritage with the layoffs. For the 4.8 million-strong Indian-American community, the episode is a reminder that proximity to power does not insulate against prejudice — and that the line between legitimate policy debate and racial scapegoating can collapse in a single news cycle.
